questions.text: Which description best matches AIGLX in a Linux graphical system?
options: A service that schedules cron jobs
An approach enabling accelerated indirect GLX, helping composited desktop effects
questions.correctAnswer: An approach enabling accelerated indirect GLX, helping composited desktop effects
questions.explanation:
AIGLX is a graphics technology that enables accelerated indirect OpenGL rendering in X environments.

Why: It relates to desktop 3D/compositing, not file storage or networking.

Example: A compositing window manager can use graphics acceleration for visual desktop effects.

Student note: AIGLX is older X11-era terminology; do not confuse it with PXE.

questions.text: A GNOME 3 user needs a desktop feature that is not included by default. What is a sensible first action?
options: Install a compatible GNOME Shell extension or use available settings
questions.correctAnswer: Install a compatible GNOME Shell extension or use available settings

Example: A window-management extension can change the desktop workflow.

questions.text: In Bash's default Emacs-style line editor, which shortcut cuts from the cursor to the end of the current line?
questions.correctAnswer: Ctrl+K
questions.explanation:
Readline provides keyboard shortcuts for editing a command before running it.

Why: Ctrl+K is kill-line, which removes text from the cursor forward.

Example: Place the cursor before '.log' in a long command and use Ctrl+K to remove the remainder.

Student note: 'Kill' here means cut text into a kill ring; it does not terminate a Linux process.

questions.text: Which default readline shortcut removes text from the cursor back to the beginning of the command line?
questions.correctAnswer: Ctrl+U
questions.explanation:
Ctrl+U cuts the text before the cursor in Bash's default Emacs-style editing mode.

Why: It operates backward to the beginning, unlike Ctrl+K.

Example: If a mistyped command begins with a wrong path, Ctrl+U removes the part before your cursor.

Student note: The shell may be configured with another editing mode, such as vi.

questions.text: You want to cut the preceding word while editing a Bash command. Which key combination is commonly used?
questions.correctAnswer: Ctrl+W
questions.explanation:
In Bash's default editing mode, Ctrl+W removes the previous word.

Why: This is a word-level edit rather than deleting the whole line.

Example: In 'cat /var/log/old.log', position the cursor after the filename and press Ctrl+W.

Student note: Ctrl+L clears the visible terminal; it does not cut a word.

questions.text: Which shortcut normally cuts the following word in the default Bash line editor?
questions.correctAnswer: Alt+D (Meta+D)
questions.explanation:
Alt+D deletes the word ahead of the cursor in Emacs-style readline.

Why: Meta is normally the Alt key; Esc then D can often be used instead.

Example: Move to the start of an incorrect argument and use Alt+D to remove it.

Student note: Ctrl+C interrupts a running command and is not the word-cut shortcut.

questions.text: After cutting a command-line fragment using a readline shortcut, which key pastes it back?
questions.correctAnswer: Ctrl+Y
questions.explanation:
Readline calls restoring recently killed text 'yanking'.

Why: Ctrl+Y inserts the most recently cut fragment.

Example: Use Ctrl+K accidentally, then Ctrl+Y to restore the cut text.

Student note: This is different from Ctrl+V, which has another purpose in many terminals.

study.remember: Ctrl+Y inserts the most recently cut fragment.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of PXE?
options: To boot a machine through a network before its installed OS starts
questions.correctAnswer: To boot a machine through a network before its installed OS starts
questions.explanation:
Preboot Execution Environment lets suitable firmware obtain boot information over the network.

Why: It is used for provisioning or booting systems without relying on a local OS installation.

Example: An IT lab can network-boot many PCs into an operating-system installer.

Student note: DHCP commonly supplies network/boot details; a server provides the boot program.

study.pitfall: DHCP commonly supplies network/boot details; a server provides the boot program.
study.remember: It is used for provisioning or booting systems without relying on a local OS installation.

keyTerms.meaning: Preboot Execution Environment lets suitable firmware obtain boot information over the network.

questions.text: After running CITY=Polokwane in Bash, which command prints the stored value?
questions.correctAnswer: echo $CITY
questions.explanation:
A shell variable holds data; a dollar sign normally asks the shell to expand it to its value.

Why: $CITY becomes Polokwane, while CITY without the dollar sign is just text.

Example: echo "$CITY" prints Polokwane.

Student note: Quotes matter: single quotes prevent normal variable expansion.

steps: $CITY becomes Polokwane, while CITY without the dollar sign is just text.

study.remember: $CITY becomes Polokwane, while CITY without the dollar sign is just text.

questions.text: Why is the sticky bit useful on a writable shared directory such as /tmp?
options: It limits deletion/renaming of entries to owners or privileged users despite shared write access
It forces all programs to run as root
questions.correctAnswer: It limits deletion/renaming of entries to owners or privileged users despite shared write access
questions.explanation:
On directories, the sticky bit restricts which users can remove or rename entries.

Why: It helps prevent one user deleting another person's files in a shared writable directory.

Example: /tmp is commonly shown with permissions such as drwxrwxrwt.

Student note: A lowercase t in the others-execute position shows sticky plus execute; T shows sticky without that execute bit.

study.title: Sticky bit
study.simple: On directories, the sticky bit restricts which users can remove or rename entries.
steps: It helps prevent one user deleting another person's files in a shared writable directory.

study.pitfall: A lowercase t in the others-execute position shows sticky plus execute; T shows sticky without that execute bit.
study.remember: It helps prevent one user deleting another person's files in a shared writable directory.

keyTerms.meaning: On directories, the sticky bit restricts which users can remove or rename entries.

questions.text: A Linux 'ls -l' permission string ends with '+'. What should you investigate?
options: Extended access-control information such as a POSIX ACL
questions.correctAnswer: Extended access-control information such as a POSIX ACL
questions.explanation:
An access control list (ACL) can grant more detailed permissions than owner/group/other bits.

Why: GNU ls commonly displays a '+' after permission bits when an ACL is present.

Example: Use getfacl filename to inspect entries for a named user.

Student note: Do not assume the visible rwx triplets show every effective permission.

study.simple: An access control list (ACL) can grant more detailed permissions than owner/group/other bits.
steps: GNU ls commonly displays a '+' after permission bits when an ACL is present.
study.example: Use getfacl filename to inspect entries for a named user.
study.pitfall: Do not assume the visible rwx triplets show every effective permission.
study.remember: GNU ls commonly displays a '+' after permission bits when an ACL is present.

keyTerms.meaning: An access control list (ACL) can grant more detailed permissions than owner/group/other bits.

questions.text: What does the Linux mount command do?
options: Adds a filesystem to the directory tree at a mount point
questions.correctAnswer: Adds a filesystem to the directory tree at a mount point
questions.explanation:
Linux exposes mounted filesystems within one directory hierarchy.

Why: Mount attaches a filesystem to a chosen directory (mount point).

Example: A prepared /dev/sdb1 might be mounted on /mnt/data.

Student note: The directory must exist, and an incorrect device choice can cause problems.

questions.text: A removable drive must be writable from both common Linux and Windows desktops. Which design concern matters most?
options: Pick the filesystem only by its colour
Select a filesystem both platforms can read/write, considering size and permission limits
Always use a native Linux-only filesystem
questions.correctAnswer: Select a filesystem both platforms can read/write, considering size and permission limits
questions.explanation:
Filesystem choice should reflect the devices and operating systems sharing the drive.

Why: A cross-platform filesystem may be more convenient but may not preserve normal Unix permissions.

Example: exFAT is often used for removable drives shared between modern Linux and Windows systems.

Student note: ext4 is a common native Linux filesystem; compatibility is a separate decision.

questions.text: With umask 022, what are the usual starting permissions for a new regular file made with mode 666?
questions.explanation:
umask removes selected permission bits from the mode requested when a file is created.

Why: 666 masked by 022 gives 644: owner read/write; group and others read.

Example: New directories normally start from 777, so with umask 022 they become 755.

Student note: Ordinary new files do not normally start executable: do not subtract the mask from 777 for files.

questions.text: What is the main group-related effect of setting the setgid bit on a shared directory?
options: Newly created entries generally inherit the directory's group
Only root can enter the directory
questions.correctAnswer: Newly created entries generally inherit the directory's group
questions.explanation:
The setgid bit on a directory supports group ownership for collaborative work.

Why: New files and subdirectories generally inherit its group, subject to filesystem behaviour.

Example: A team's shared folder can use chmod g+s and group write permissions.

Student note: Setgid does not replace correct access permissions or ACLs.

questions.text: Which command most directly summarises how much disk space /var/log uses in human-readable units?
questions.correctAnswer: du -sh /var/log
questions.explanation:

Why: It answers the space-consumption question for one directory.

Example: du -sh /var/log might report 1.2G.

questions.text: Scenario: A training centre must install Linux on 20 PCs using a network rather than individual USB sticks. Explain a sensible PXE-based workflow and name the main parts involved.
questions.correctAnswer: Enable network/PXE boot in client firmware; configure DHCP to provide IP and boot information; provide suitable boot files over TFTP or another supported boot method; load an installer or network image; ensure reachable network and compatible architecture; test on one machine before scaling.
aiRubric: Identifies PXE/network boot and firmware option
Mentions delivery of a bootloader or boot program (for example TFTP)
questions.aiReferenceNotes: Network boot can install many systems from centrally maintained boot resources. Prepare compatible network-boot image and boot services. Configure DHCP and the boot-file service as required by the environment. Enable network boot on the clients and validate on one machine before rollout. A lab boots to a network installer that loads its files from the deployment server. Network boot is not the same as mounting an already-running machine's remote filesystem.
questions.explanation:
Network boot can install many systems from centrally maintained boot resources.

Method:
1. Prepare compatible network-boot image and boot services.
2. Configure DHCP and the boot-file service as required by the environment.
3. Enable network boot on the clients and validate on one machine before rollout.

Example: A lab boots to a network installer that loads its files from the deployment server.

Student note: Network boot is not the same as mounting an already-running machine's remote filesystem.

questions.text: Scenario: Two colleagues need extra access to a single Linux file without changing access for everyone in the file's group. Describe how to check and manage suitable permissions.
questions.correctAnswer: Inspect ls -l and getfacl; retain normal owner/group/other permissions; add a suitable named-user ACL entry with setfacl -m u:username:rw file as appropriate; check the effective permissions and ACL mask with getfacl; use least privilege.
aiRubric: Identifies ACL as granular permission mechanism
Mentions ACL mask/effective rights or least privilege
questions.aiReferenceNotes: ACLs can permit named users or groups when ordinary rwx permission groups are too broad. Check ownership and existing access before changing anything. Grant only the necessary rights to the named user using setfacl. Verify the effective ACL and test access with the intended account. setfacl -m u:thabo:rw report.txt adds an entry for thabo; getfacl report.txt shows the result. A '+' after ls -l mode bits is a clue, not a full permission explanation.
questions.explanation:
ACLs can permit named users or groups when ordinary rwx permission groups are too broad.

Method:
1. Check ownership and existing access before changing anything.
2. Grant only the necessary rights to the named user using setfacl.
3. Verify the effective ACL and test access with the intended account.

Example: setfacl -m u:thabo:rw report.txt adds an entry for thabo; getfacl report.txt shows the result.

Student note: A '+' after ls -l mode bits is a clue, not a full permission explanation.

study.title: Granular file permissions
study.simple: ACLs can permit named users or groups when ordinary rwx permission groups are too broad.
steps: Check ownership and existing access before changing anything.
Grant only the necessary rights to the named user using setfacl.
Verify the effective ACL and test access with the intended account.
study.example: setfacl -m u:thabo:rw report.txt adds an entry for thabo; getfacl report.txt shows the result.
study.pitfall: A '+' after ls -l mode bits is a clue, not a full permission explanation.
study.remember: Check ownership and existing access before changing anything.

keyTerms.meaning: ACLs can permit named users or groups when ordinary rwx permission groups are too broad.

questions.text: Scenario: A new data partition should be available at /srv/data after every reboot. Explain a safe preparation, mount and persistence process.
questions.correctAnswer: Confirm the device and partition using lsblk -f and blkid; back up any existing data; format only if appropriate; create /srv/data; test mounting; record its UUID and filesystem type in /etc/fstab with suitable options; validate with mount -a and df/findmnt, taking care not to overwrite data.
aiRubric: Explains mount point creation and trial mount
Validates configuration and notes data-loss risk
questions.aiReferenceNotes: A mount links a filesystem to a directory; /etc/fstab describes mounts to arrange automatically. Identify the right partition and its UUID. Mount it to an existing directory and check its content. Add a tested fstab entry, then verify with mount -a. An entry can use UUID=... /srv/data ext4 defaults 0 2 for a suitable ext4 data filesystem. Formatting destroys existing filesystem contents; mounting and formatting are different tasks.
questions.explanation:
A mount links a filesystem to a directory; /etc/fstab describes mounts to arrange automatically.

Method:
1. Identify the right partition and its UUID.
2. Mount it to an existing directory and check its content.
3. Add a tested fstab entry, then verify with mount -a.

Example: An entry can use UUID=... /srv/data ext4 defaults 0 2 for a suitable ext4 data filesystem.

Student note: Formatting destroys existing filesystem contents; mounting and formatting are different tasks.

questions.text: A company wants to reuse an open-source component in a product it distributes. Explain why it must compare a strong copyleft licence with a permissive licence before deciding.
questions.correctAnswer: The company must read the exact licence and distribution obligations; strong copyleft licences such as GPL generally require source/compatible licensing of covered derivative distributed works, while permissive licences such as MIT generally allow wider reuse with copyright and licence notices. The obligations depend on the version, combination and way software is distributed; seek legal review when needed.
aiRubric: Defines source-code/licence obligations at a useful level
Mentions keeping required copyright or licence notices
Notes distribution and exact licence terms matter
questions.aiReferenceNotes: Open-source does not mean no conditions; licences specify what users can modify and redistribute. Identify every component and its exact licence/version. Check notice, source availability and redistribution obligations. Record compliance for the intended form of product distribution. A distributed application that includes GPL-covered code needs a different compliance review from one that includes an MIT-licensed library. This is licence-awareness practice, not legal advice; do not assume all open-source licences have the same obligations.
